summary: An inequality compares expressions and, unlike an equation, its solution is a RANGE (a set) of values rather than a single value. On a number line that range is shown by a circle at the boundary — open/hollow for strict < or > (boundary excluded), closed/filled for inclusive ≤ or ≥ (boundary included) — with an arrow or segment covering the values that satisfy it. Solving uses the same inverse operations as equations, except that multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the inequality sign (an extension point). The core skill is translating fluently among a worded constraint, the inequality symbol and the number-line diagram, tying circle style to boundary inclusion, the arrow to the satisfying set, and rehearsing worded phrases such as 'at least' and 'at most'.
misconceptions: Confuses strict (<, >) with inclusive (≤, ≥): uses the wrong circle style (open for ≥, filled for <).
Shades or points the arrow the wrong way (reads the symbol direction backwards).
Treats the solution as a single boundary value (x < 5 means x = 4) rather than a whole set.
Worded-boundary error: renders 'at least 12' as x > 12 (strict) instead of x ≥ 12.

activities.title: Build and test a number-line inequality
steps: Choose an inequality symbol (<, ≤, >, ≥) and a boundary value, then draw the matching number line: decide whether the boundary circle is open or closed and which way the arrow points.
Test several sample values by asking of each, 'does this value satisfy the inequality?', and mark those that satisfy it (e.g. in one colour) and those that do not (another colour).

Switch the symbol from ≥ to > (or ≤ to <) on the same boundary and observe what changes: the boundary circle hollows, and a value sitting exactly on the boundary flips from satisfying to not satisfying.
Deliberately draw the arrow the wrong way, then test values along it to see that a whole stretch of the line fails the check — confirming direction matters.
Read a given diagram (e.g. a filled circle at −2 with a right-pointing arrow) back into symbols and words.
activities.insight: Inclusion is not an arbitrary drawing convention: whether the circle is filled depends on whether the boundary value itself is a solution. The arrow/segment represents the whole set of satisfying values, and its direction is fixed by what the symbol means.

activities.title: Translate worded constraints into symbols and diagrams
steps: Translate worded constraints into inequality symbols: 'at least 12' → x ≥ 12, 'at most'/'no more than' → ≤, 'more than' → strict >, 'less than' → strict <.
Build a phrase→symbol reference table and, for each phrase, test the boundary value against the words ('is 12 allowed if you must be at least 12?').
Draw the number-line diagram for a compound statement such as 'x is at least 1 and less than 4' (closed circle at 1, open circle at 4, segment shaded between).
Check your diagram by reading it back into words and comparing with the original statement.
activities.insight: Everyday boundary phrases map precisely onto strict or inclusive symbols, and testing whether the boundary value is allowed decides between an open and closed circle.

activities.title: Solve a simple linear inequality and plot its solution set
steps: Solve a one-step or two-step inequality such as 3x + 1 < 10 using the same inverse operations as an equation (subtract 1, then divide by 3, giving x < 3).
Represent the resulting solution set on a number line with the correct open or closed circle and arrow.
Check the solution by testing a value inside the range and a value outside it.
(Extension) Explore what happens when both sides are multiplied or divided by a negative number, using test values to discover that the inequality direction reverses.
activities.insight: Solving an inequality mirrors solving an equation, but the answer is a set shown on the number line; special care is needed when multiplying or dividing by a negative because the direction reverses.

activities.title: Reference card: symbols, circles and directions
steps: Match each of <, ≤, >, ≥ to its circle style (open for strict, closed for inclusive) and, for inequalities written with the variable on the left (e.g. x < 3), to the direction of its arrow; notice that 3 > x means the same as x < 3, so the arrow still points left.
Use the card as a check when building or reading diagrams, confirming each choice against whether the boundary value is itself a solution.
activities.insight: The four symbols map systematically onto circle style; they map onto arrow direction once the inequality is written with the variable on the left (e.g. x ≥ a points right), giving a quick self-check reference.

checkQuestion: Here is a number line with a FILLED (closed) circle at −2 and an arrow pointing to the right. First: what inequality does this diagram show? Then, on a fresh number line, show the solution to the statement 'x is at least 1 and less than 4'.
checkAnswer: The diagram shows x ≥ −2 (closed circle = boundary included; arrow to the right = values greater than or equal to −2). The produced number line has a CLOSED circle at 1, an OPEN circle at 4, and the segment between them shaded: 1 ≤ x < 4.
